research on indoor positioning systems has intensified, considering or rejecting the use of GPS signals.  This study focuses on developing a GPS-assisted indoor positioning system, leveraging the global navigation satellite system's widespread availability and accurate external location data.  Initially, a model is proposed to estimate indoor receiver positions based on observed GPS signals, utilizing the minimal distance concept with unknown external locations.  Then, an iterative algorithm is introduced to determine external locations and optimize indoor receiver positions simultaneously, building on the non-linear least squares method.  To evaluate the system's performance, comprehensive simulations are conducted under various conditions, indicating that the system's accuracy improves significantly with additional GPS observations, as expected. Furthermore, the system's efficiency is demonstrated by simulations, paving the way for its implementation on computational devices.  To facilitate real-world testing, a prototype of the proposed system is also outlined, consisting of a multi-agent architecture and a cloud-based data processing system, which can be developed using widely available technologies.  Ultimately, this research offers a viable solution for developing GPS-assisted indoor positioning systems, with potential applications including smart buildings and indoor navigation systems.  The system's source code is available online for researchers to build upon and improve.

Our proposed multi-way translation model uses a shared neural network with multiple input and output pairs of languages, while surpassing the benchmark of summing the performance of each individual bilingual model. This process has been successfully implemented with the help of a two-mode squeezed vacuum (TMZV) state, commonly referred to as the SPS circuit. Here, we propose a different approach to achieve SPS using a pair of entangled mirrors that reflect a photon from a given state. The implementation of fits to generate probability density functions for virtual signal cross-sections and other parameters is common practice; however, the assumptions behind this method are not widely known. This article clarifies the underlying theory used to derive these PDFs and discusses uncertainty quantification methods. We introduce the concept of a covariance matrix that adequately captures the uncertainty in question and provide a formula to calculate it. This calculation is then applied to typical nuisance parameters such as luminosity, flux, and efficiency. The article also discusses factors that influence the uncertainty of cross-sections, including flux and efficiency parameters, as well as the behavior of cross-section fits under different conditions. We discuss the practice of threshold-lowering and its impact on the uncertainty of cross-sections.   chain of spins experiencing a sudden, uniform change in temperature, and a 
  similar scenario involving a quasi-one-dimensional spin chain with a gradient 
  in temperature. In both cases, we develop a theoretical framework to measure T- 
  fluctuations and apply it to predict the emergence of observable T-fluctuations. 
  Our analysis includes an in-depth examination of the spin chain with a gradient 
  in temperature and an assessment of the feasibility of experimenting on a one- 
  dimensional, finite chain of spins. 
  Methods. We employ a multi-component Glauber model and derive an expression 
  for the T-fluctuation operator. To study T-fluctuations in these systems, 
  we integrate the Glauber model with the two-state system that drives the T- 
  fluctuations. This integration enables us to derive an equation for the T- 
  fluctuations and use it to analyze the conditions under which these fluctuations 
  become macroscopically observable. 
  Results. We demonstrate that in both scenarios, the T-fluctuations will 
  eventually return to their equilibrium form following the change in temperature,

  fluctuations in the chain with a gradient in temperature will also return to

  identified the conditions under which they will be observable. Our study

Agents of this type are effective at completing tasks consistently when given a set of preselected actions, obtained through random trial and error. We have improved this capability by enhancing their ability to discover new action lists automatically, using a combination of reward reinforcement learning and a statistical tool that identifies the most coherent patterns. As a result, agents now learn action lists in half the time and with greater consistency, leading to an overall improvement of 25% in their performance. Ultimately, this method enables the discovery of intricate action lists that achieve remarkable results, such as outperforming human opponents in a simple game, and navigating through the majority of levels in a challenging obstacle course. We have also developed a metric that measures the complexity of action lists and discovered that agents learn these lists in a orderly, step-by-step fashion. For example, in a simple game, the action list learned first allows the agent to move one step, and then subsequent lists enable movements of two, three, and so steps, until the agent reaches the goal. We have also discovered that agents learn action lists in a hierarchical manner, and that each list builds upon the previous one, by incorporating new actions at the same time as existing ones, a phenomenon we term 'layered generalization'. We demonstrate the applicability of our method to the discovery of action lists in multiple environments and tasks, and provide a proposal for future research aimed at exploring the role of cognition models in this process. We have found that our method excels in scenarios where action lists learn quickly, but also discovered a limitation in our research, where action lists learn slowly in environments with unstable rewards, a challenge we aim to tackle in the future, and attribute this difficulty to the need for our agents to re-evaluate their existing actions when confronted with new ones, a problem we term the 'action re-evaluation problem'. Specifically, our proof demonstrates that successful solutions to BRRLE can be applied to break the quantum ring learning with errors (QRLWE) problem, and conversely, successful solutions to QRLWE can be applied to break BRRLE. This equivalence provides a direct connection between two decisional problems that were previously considered distinct. Furthermore, we demonstrate that BRRLE is computationally equivalent to two other problems: ring learning with errors (RLWE) and the quantum ring learning with errors (QRLWE) problem, which can solve a specific hidden subset sum problem. Specifically, our proof demonstrates that successful solutions to BRRLE can be applied to break an instance of an RLWE or QRLWE problem, and in return, successful solutions to an RLWE or QRLWE problem can be applied to break a BRRLE problem. This equivalence is the foundation for our proposal of a BRRLE problem as a secure and efficient quantumly-verifiable problem. Specifically, our proposal demonstrates that successful solutions to an BRRLE problem can be applied to break an instance of both a hidden subset sum problem and a quantumly-verifiable problem, which can be witnessed by a quantumly-verifiable circuit that consists of both a BRRLE circuit and a quantumly-verifiable transformation circuit, which transforms BRRLE outputs into quantumly-verifiable outputs, such as QRLWE problem outputs. This circuit can be executed both efficiently classically and quantumly. The development of unbiased estimators for evaluating multiple objectives simultaneously has allowed researchers to compare models incorporating additional tasks into the generation process. However, these estimators require expensive computations and are only applicable to batched training. In response to these limitations, we propose new unbiased estimators for evaluating multiple objectives using mini-batches. These estimators are highly efficient, versatile, and adaptable to both batched and mini-batched training. In our experiments, we show that these estimators facilitate the development of efficient image synthesis models, particularly those incorporating additional tasks, and yield consistent performance improvements. In particular, one such model achieves a Fisher information bound of 2.95 dB, surpassing the previous state-of-the-art of 3.29 dB. In addition, our findings highlight the advantage of efficient models in handling large datasets. In total, our work provides researchers with more effective tools to explore innovative image synthesis architectures. We establish that when the incident angle lies within a certain critical range, the unique continuation principle can be applied without restriction, while outside this range, a growth of order O(k^-1) in the incident wave number k is required to achieve quantitative results. This is demonstrated through a combination of local uniqueness estimates and the direct use of the Green's function, in addition to an modified version of the boundary layer method. Specifically, for oblique angles greater than the critical value, we prove that if data on a finite segment of the boundary differ by less than ε, then the corresponding inhomogeneities also exhibit a difference of magnitude O(ε) within a distance of approximately ε^(1/2)k^(1/2) from the boundary, provided that the wave number k is sufficiently large. This provides a quantitative interpretation of the local uniqueness estimate initially obtained by Imanuvilnem in 1985. On the other hand, for angles greater than the critical value by any nonzero amount, we establish that there exist counterexamples showing the failure of direct extension of the previous result to yield an explicit bound on the distance from the boundary at which the difference between two inhomogeneous media can be determined from the corresponding boundary data with a given precision ε, regardless of the wave number k. Consequently, this indicates that the growth rate O(k^-1) in the modified result is optimal. Furthermore, we demonstrate the feasibility of our approach by deriving a novel bound on the Green's function that is applicable to frequencies both within and outside the high-frequency regime, thus yielding an explicit bound on the distance from the boundary at the rate O(ε^(1/2)k^(1/2)). This bound is employed to establish the required local uniqueness estimate, which in turn forms the basis for the application of the boundary layer method. In particular, we obtain an explicit bound on the local uniqueness estimate of order O(ε^(1/2)k^(1/2)), which is shown to be sufficient for the original problem of quantitative unique continuation, while the counterexamples mentioned earlier indicate that this bound is insufficient for the modified problem when the angle is within the critical range by any nonzero amount.

Typically, recommender systems can be viewed as bipartite networks, where users and items are distinct entities connected by edges representing user-item interactions.  However, many real-world applications involve additional items, such as categories or sub-items, which complicate the network structure.  To address this complexity, a common practice is to reduce these additional items to representative items, effectively simplifying the network.  In contrast, our proposed Multi-Relational Attributed Graph (MRAG) framework, incorporates multiple relationships between users, items, and their attributes, without collapsing these attributes.  Specifically, MRAG treats user-item interactions as separate entities, rather than connecting users directly to items.  We demonstrate the effectiveness of the MRAG framework by developing a comprehensive model that leverages multiple relations and attributed information, and experimentally show its performance surpasses current state-of-the-art methods.  Our results indicate that the MRAG framework's ability to safely share user and item data, without needing to combine them, significantly enhances the recommendability of each item, outperforming existing methods by an average 7.07% on the AHRF metric.  Furthermore, we found that carefully identifying item categories can enhance the recommendation performance, with an average improvement of 6.57% on the AHRF metric, indicating future potential in studying relations and attributed information in graph-based recommender systems. an efficient controller for a swarm of unmanned aerial vehicles performing aggressive navigation in the presence of unknown winds is addressed. A dynamic controller is designed that compensates for unanticipated wind effects and ensures the swarm maintains a predetermined formation. The underlying dynamics are assumed to follow a stochastic differential inclusion, and the controller is developed using the backstepping method, resulting in a closed-loop system that can be analyzed to guarantee the swarm's ability to navigate to a desired location despite wind interference. The effectiveness of this controller is demonstrated through simulated tests using autonomous navigation and multi-agent control systems. The code is available on an open-source repository. To address the issue of using these modalities separately, there has been growing interest in concurrent capture technologies.  Capturing the 3D geometry of objects while obtaining visual features requires simultaneous processing of both domains.  For instance, structured light systems use projected light sources that are detected in camera images, necessitating simultaneous light projection and image capturing.  Similarly, radar and lidar technologies need concurrent operation to produce accurate distance measurements and visual data.  Consequently, the development of independent algorithms for subsequent data processing is inadequate, making it necessary to design end-to-end systems that integrate capture domain expertise.  Unfortunately, the wide range of possible capture techniques limits the development of universally applicable systems.  To address this challenge, we propose a general-purpose model capable of processing image and point cloud data generated by different capture techniques, thereby increasing the potential for its application across various fields such as medicine, manufacturing, and defense.  To facilitate model training, we create a comprehensive dataset containing data produced by five distinct capture techniques including laser scanning, endoscopy, radar, and both near-field and far-field microwave transmission, and demonstrate the efficacy of our model in accurately performing classification, detection, and segmentation tasks using data produced by these techniques. Despite being a fundamental approach, constructing a supervised EEG classification system faces significant challenges due to highly expressive signal features and their inherent interdependence. To address this issue, this study proposes an approach based on sparse models, including a method for evaluating and displaying the resulting time-dependent feature importance.  This approach is useful for identifying time-dependent brain regions involved in specific cognitive tasks and could serve as a reliable alternative to existing methods.  By processing a comprehensive dataset containing 124 electrodes and five cognitive tasks, our method successfully extracted time-dependent feature importance information, demonstrating its practical utility.  Furthermore, our proposed technique outperformed established methods, demonstrating superior performance in EEG classification tasks.  This approach's code is freely accessible for use by other researchers.  In addition to enhancing understanding of time-dependent brain region involvement in cognitive processes, this study's findings provide a reliable feature importance framework that can be applied to other EEG datasets.  In particular, we investigated the N-back, task-switching, and working memory tasks using the SAMN dataset, which included data from 34 young adults.  Each participant completed three cognitive tasks while their EEG was recorded.  In the N-back task, participants identified whether presented stimuli matched previously seen ones, one (simple N-back) or two (dual N-back) presentations earlier.  Task-switching involved alternating between N-back tasks of different lengths.  Working memory capacity was measured using the Auditory Continuous Performance Task (ACPT).  We constructed a classification system using 124 electrodes and analyzed time-dependent feature importance in the frequency and time domains.  To evaluate our method's effectiveness, we applied two techniques: a weighted sum of individual importance values and a non-negative matrix factorization-based method. irected Treewidth Inference (GDTI) by effectively utilizing it to find optimal orderings for Binary Decision Diagrams (BDDs), particularly in cases where computationally expensive predicates are involved. Typically, BDDs are optimized through a bottom-up traversal, known as the "reordering heuristic," which aims to minimize the BDD's size by choosing efficient predicates. However, this approach can be time-consuming when complex predicates are present, making it inefficient for large models and formulas. In contrast, our approach leverages GDTI's ability to efficiently determine the optimal order for BDDs, achieving significant performance improvements (up to 100 times faster computation) when compared to the conventional reordering heuristic. Moreover, our orderings produce smaller BDDs, resulting in substantial time savings (up to 5000 times) when compared to the conventional reordering heuristic. We demonstrate our findings using a suite of benchmarks featuring linear arithmetic formulas, solved with the Z3 satisfiability solver, and show that our approach produces both smaller and more efficient BDDs. Our technique has potential applications in scenarios where BDDs are commonly employed, including computer-aided design, cryptography, and machine learning. 

  We further demonstrate that in some cases, particularly with linear arithmetic and hash functions, the optimal order corresponds to the order in which variables appear in the input formula or model. In such cases, the best order can be derived effortlessly from the input, rendering the computationally expensive GDTI method unnecessary. Nonetheless, our research reveals that even when the optimal order is already present, employing GDTI still yields significant performance benefits (up to 10 times faster computation) when computing the BDD, as opposed to the alternative approach of constructing the BDD in the given order and then applying it to queries. 

  We also explore and evaluate additional ordering heuristics, including a simple predicate-based heuristic, along with combining GDTI with the conventional reordering heuristic, which yields modest improvements (up to 2 times faster computation) when compared to the computationally expensive GDTI method. Nevertheless, the primary contribution of our research remains the efficient utilization of GDTI for BDD order optimization.

Specifically, we examine how imperfections in the boundary affect the scattering matrix and investigate the statistical properties of the reflection matrix in the case of weak imperfections. Our analysis focuses on a quantum billiard enclosed within an elliptical path and reveals that minor deviations in the boundary have a significant impact on the scattering matrix, resulting in a non-episodic behavior. Furthermore, we find that when the boundary imperfections are weak, the reflection matrix exhibits random characteristics, except for a few distinct channels. We derive an explicit expression for the scattering matrix and confirm that it aligns with the results obtained through an experimental demonstration. Additionally, we explore the non-perfect boundary effects on the horizon and the separation of dynamic phases. Our findings demonstrate that minor deviations in the boundary can significantly impact the scattering matrix, resulting in a non-episodic behavior, and leading to over-shadowing in some channels, and also influence the separation of dynamic phases, and the shape of the horizon. Recent research indicates that even small, high-quality models can achieve remarkable performance when employing techniques like few-shot learning.  In this context, creating high-quality datasets for fine-tuning these models becomes increasingly important.  Web-based data generation campaigns, like the one we present with WikiEntities-38, involve building large datasets consisting of 38 basic entity types by leveraging the content of Wikipedia.  We develop and apply a customized annotation framework to create WikiEntities-38, a dataset containing 3.7 million entity-based instructions and related text passages.  Evaluations using the T0 model demonstrate that even without explicit entity-aware training, fine-tuning on WikiEntities-38 leads to notable improvements in the MultiWE entity-based inference benchmark, specifically a 6.5% increase in the F1 score.  Our research highlights the value of large-scale web-based data generation in NLP.  Building upon WikiEntities-38, we introduce additional datasets covering 11 additional entity types, along with corresponding data generation challenges.  These additional entities focus on more complex categories such as relationships and categorizations, requiring further research into efficient data-efficient fine-tuning methods.  Our work incorporates a publicly accessible repository containing the necessary code, datasets, and models for community evaluation and improvement.  We anticipate that these datasets and associated models will contribute positively to the advancement of multi-entity inference within NLP. This task is known as multi-person multi-event analysis. Recent studies

a score-based unsupervised boundary learning technique, 
wherein the primary event detection module is trained independently, 
and the boundary learning module is trained separately 
using unsupervised boundary samples generated based 
on the scores from the RNN components, including the EPAN and 
a previous multi-event detection module. This score-based 
approach replaces complex bidirectional connections 
between the detection and analysis modules with 
more efficient single-directional connections, 
enabling the system to process videos in a pipeline manner. 
Experimental results show this proposed system performs 
better than existing multi-event analysis approaches 
and rivals top single-event analysis models, 
with the added benefit of being real-time capable.

an annotated multi-person multi-event dataset,

We establish a new stability criterion, applicable to dark solitons in two-dimensional space, which is based on a specific integral test. This new criterion is more flexible than a previous stability condition, which relied on the norm, and we demonstrate that it is closely related to the notion of norm stability. Additionally, we investigate the local stability of dark solitons in three-dimensional space, which is characterized by a non-fluctuation dynamics, and we derive an explicit stability condition expressed in terms of a surface energy functional. This new condition is more detailed than a previous condition, which was expressed in terms of the norm, and it is more flexible, which is essential for achieving local stability of dark solitons. We demonstrate that both of the new stability conditions can yield explicit lower bounds on the parameter $c$ that characterizes a dark soliton, which is a solution of the nonlinear wave equation. Furthermore, we show that both of these lower bounds can be optimized numerically using the interval or surface integral test, which provides a precise lower bound on $c$ for which a dark soliton is stable, which is essential for dark solitons used in experiments at the BEC facility in Vienna.

the galaxy itself, as observed in the far-infrared to millimeter wave

We also demonstrated the benefits of incorporating temperature data instead of discarding it, and found that the model's performance can be optimized with the proposed loss function.  Additionally, we examined the model's robustness to varying temperatures and illumination conditions.  With efficient parameter utilization, our proposed framework offers a viable solution for incorporating thermal to visible face recognition in real-world applications.  We have made our code and data available at https://github.com/ycszen/self-balanced-triplet-loss.  In particular, our findings indicate that a considerable temperature difference (at least 38 K) is necessary for the model to effectively learn from the temperature data in conjunction with the visual information.  Consequently, a minimal amount of necessary temperature data (only 0.1 K) can be sufficient when the temperature difference is substantial.  Moreover, our proposed framework excels in scenarios with moderate changes in temperature and illumination conditions, and mainly relies on the visual information when there is substantial illumination variation. These problems involve finding conditions under which given $k$-arcs in a finite field $F_q$ satisfy certain incidence relationships with a specific subset of the field. We establish a connection between these conditions and binary linear codes of length $n=3m$, focusing on the image weights of code automorphisms. Specifically, for each of the three known cases in characteristic two, we identify the desired conditions as equivalent to the nonexistence of a particular binary linear code, or as being closely related to the properties of another binary linear code. We also explore the implications of these connections in the context of the nonexistence or possible construction of certain binary linear codes. This research extends previous work on Cameron-Liebler problems in characteristic two, and provides a more comprehensive understanding of the relationship between these problems and binary linear codes. This relationship is particularly useful as it enables us to apply recent advances in binary linear codes to address open questions related to $k$-arcs in finite fields in characteristic two. This, in turn, facilitates the construction of larger sets of $k$-arcs satisfying the given incidence conditions, or the determination of upper bounds for the number of such sets. This construction or bound is expressed in terms of the size of the finite field $F_q$. The three cases we consider involve $k$-arcs that are subspaces, $k$-arcs with a specific singular exterior, or $k$-arcs within a particular hyperplane. The nonexistence of certain binary linear codes is equivalent to the existence of an infinite number of $k$-arcs of the specified type in a given finite field $F_q$. The image weights of the code automorphisms are also considered, specifically in the cases of a quadratic code of length $2^m$, a Golay code of length $2^m$, or a Hamming code of length $3m$. A key component in the speech generation process is the additive white Gaussian noise (AWGN) model used for analyzing and synthesizing speech, often taken as a given in previous studies.  However, the underlying assumptions of these models are not universally applicable, especially for non-linear systems, which is a subject of ongoing research.  This paper presents a mathematical derivation of the speech synthesis error, which previous researchers had assumed to be Gaussian, along with a subsequent investigation into the stationarity and parameter estimation techniques of the speech synthesis model.  We demonstrate that the speech synthesis model is non-stationary and propose an effective method for estimating its parameters.  To validate our findings, a speech coding experiment was conducted using a 64 kbps vector quantizer, with the results indicating that the non-stationarity of the speech synthesis model has a negligible impact on sound quality, but the parameters of the speech synthesis model influence sound quality when speech is synthesized using the model.  Consequently, updating the model periodically can improve sound quality without increasing the bit rate.  In particular, the results show that periodic updating of the parameters of the speech synthesis model reduces quality degradation by half when high-bit-rate speech is downsampled.  The non-stationarity of the speech synthesis model implies that speech and synthesis must be segmented into frames of the same duration, which presents a challenge for efficient implementation.  Despite these difficulties, the results indicate that the effort is worthwhile, with the best trade-off between complexity and quality achieved with frames of 30 ms duration.  The findings of this research are applicable to both optimal and near-optimal quantizers, with the exception that optimal quantizers are only practical for short frames.  The conclusion drawn from this study is that accurate sound quality in speech coding depends on a thorough understanding of the speech synthesis model, which is essential for the development of speech coding algorithms requiring high quality.  In such applications as telephony, where quality is critical, speech coding algorithms are primary research objectives, otherwise they are secondary to bit rate constraints. core-collapse supernovae are both major celestial events that significantly impact their surroundings, affecting various fields including astrophysics and cosmology. Furthermore, the potential connection between some supernovae and GRBs suggests that understanding these interactions is crucial. This study presents new models based on the first-order fluid approximation, accounting for the influence of relativistic electrons on the magnetic field in long-duration GRBs with an external magnetic field. By utilizing the test-field approximation, the reformulated transport equation for relativistic electrons is simplified, resulting in a consistent description of electron and magnetic field behavior. The developed models are applied to observe the effects on multi-dimensional simulations of supernovae and GRBs. The findings indicate that the external magnetic field has a limited impact on the supernova explosion, whereas it significantly affects the GRB behavior, influencing shock wave structure and ejecta interactions, which may reduce X-ray and gamma-ray flux. The study also discovers that the presence of an external magnetic field can enhance forward shock wave velocity, leading to an extended and brighter tail in some GRBs. The research provides a starting point for more intricate scenarios involving supernovae and GRBs, as well as other explosive phenomena involving magnetic fields. The numerical code employed in this study is publicly accessible, catering to the growing demand for realistic radiative modeling in the analysis of multi-messengers from these events. A recent breakthrough established a connection between the model's output and the format of the training data, specifically showing that a particular type of linear model's predictions reveal information about the mean and variance of the data distribution. Building upon this finding, we demonstrate that even a single Adversarial Neural Turing Machine (ANTM) model possesses a highly detailed understanding of the distribution from which data is drawn, despite being a more complex learning model. Our research reveals that the predictions made by an ANTM model that processes input and provides output in the form of a linear combination of vectors can be reversed to obtain a distribution composed of the same linear components. In other words, the linear predictions of the ANTM model accurately replicate the distribution of the training data, indicating that the manner in which data is generated is fully recoverable. We further demonstrate that multiple ANTM models can collectively reconstruct a training distribution with a high degree of precision and in real-time, allowing for the reconstitution of distributional knowledge as predictive performance declines over time. These findings highlight the transparency of ANTM models and the recoverability of training data, with practical applications in data protection and secure machine learning. However, they also introduce security threats, such as reverse engineering of models by adversaries who have access to the predictions made by the models but not the data used for training. We offer a framework for mitigating these risks, with solutions such as replacing data with synthetic data that is harder to deduce from the models' predictions, adding noise to predictions to conceal distributional information, and employing additional security measures to protect against the extraction of data from the models' linear predictions. We also examine the feasibility of these measures in scenarios involving multiple models and large datasets, with varying levels of difficulty. Ultimately, our research provides a foundation for exploring the intricacies of complex learning models and the potential exploitation of their linear predictions, with far-reaching implications for the development of more transparent and secure machine learning models. Previously, researchers have shown that in highly assortative networks, the energy levels roughly follow a pattern known as the "spectrum of free groups."  This pattern is characterized by energy levels that increase in discrete steps, with the size of these steps determined by the network's fundamental parameter, specifically its assortativity parameter.  As a result, the energy levels in these networks display an approximate linear increase with a slope proportional to the assortativity parameter.  In contrast, networks that are anti-assortative exhibit an almost linear decrease in energy levels.  Furthermore, researchers have derived an expression for the energy level differences that can be used to identify the underlying network's properties solely from the energy level data.  Additionally, we demonstrate that this degree-degree correlation has a clear impact on the network's geometry, particularly in the communities that can be seen as sub-networks, and provide a detailed analysis of this effect.  We observed that in highly assortative networks, the communities exhibit an almost uniform structure, with distinct degree steps, in contrast to anti-assortative networks where the degrees are more dispersed.  We propose that the linearity of the energy levels can be seen as a manifestation of the geometric structure of these networks, with the energy level steps representing the size of these communities.  We verified this by showing that the researchers' previous methods for identifying the linearity of energy levels, such as the variance of degree distributions within the communities, are insufficient, and that more robust methods such as the coefficient of variation are required.  We also discovered that in anti-assortative networks, the degrees within the communities are more dispersed, and that the researchers' previous study of linearity of energy levels was flawed due to the influence of outliers.  We resolved this issue by employing robust methods that are immune to the influence of isolated degree values, and found that the linearity of energy levels in anti-assortative networks is actually a decrease rather than an increase.  We propose that the distinction between increase and decrease refers to the direction of energy level shift within the communities, and that this linearity can be seen as a geometric structure effect, with the energy level steps representing the size of these communities.  We verified this by demonstrating that in anti-assortative networks, the communities exhibit more dispersed degrees, and that the linearity of energy levels is driven by this effect, and that this effect is more pronounced in smaller communities. This study extends this concept to apply it to the study of phase separation, specifically in the context of spin-flip transitions. This model exhibits quasi-long-range correlations in its ground state, making it suitable for testing quantum error correction protocols.  Our findings show that these correlations are well preserved when simulated on near-term quantum computers using quantum circuits and logical qubit encoding.  Specifically, our research demonstrates that a widely used topological code can efficiently correct errors in simulations of this model, thus providing a benchmark to test the performance of error correction in quantum simulations of quasi-long-range phenomena. This algorithm leverages the formulation of influence propagation as constraint satisfaction, and employs a novel variant of the Davis-Putnam algorithm to determine a minimum subset $S$ satisfying the influence propagation constraints. We also develop a faster, though approximate, method for finding a subset $S$ such that every node $v \in V$ is influenced by some node $u \in S$, by utilizing a variant of the conflict-driven propositional satisfiability algorithm. The approximate algorithm's performance is evaluated on large-scale random graphs generated according to various models, and the results show a significant improvement in computational efficiency compared to the exact algorithm. In our analysis, we consider the demon to be either a perfect, irreversible thermodynamic machine or subject to internal decay caused by information loss. In either case, we find that it cannot effectively utilize more than half of the available energy to create a temperature gradient. This inefficiency arises from the need to invest energy in making decisions and updating information, which results in an increase in entropy within the demon itself. As a result, the demon can only create a higher temperature gradient if the heat energy drawn from the colder region is less than the temperature gradient itself. Moreover, we find that the entropy production due to information loss is constant and contributes to the heat energy drawn from the colder region, further constraining the demon's ability to create a higher temperature gradient. These limitations ultimately prevent the demon from generating work from the gradient itself. Our analysis provides a more comprehensive understanding of the demon's inability to create a higher temperature gradient, addressing concerns that the demon's behavior may violate the second law of thermodynamics due to its alleged ability to efficiently utilize the available energy to create a temperature gradient. In fact, the demon's behavior is consistent with the increase in total entropy, which includes the entropy change within the demon itself. In the context of quantum information, we demonstrate that similar limitations apply to a two-level system with a controlled-not gate, showing that the demon's inability to create a higher temperature gradient is a universal consequence of its information-based nature. These findings highlight the fundamental challenge of using information to drive a chemical or thermal gradient efficiently. In contrast, systems that can do so efficiently, such as solar cells or fuel cells, operate in direct physical transformations that convert energy from one form to another, in contrast to the demon's information-based energy transduction. In the quantum information context, we also show that the demon's inability to create a higher temperature gradient results in an increased number of excited states that can be used to generate work, which can be achieved through a quantum reverse operation of the controlled-not gate. In this case, the work is extracted as a shift in the energy levels rather than a change in entropy, highlighting the fundamental difference between quantum and classical information and their respective energy transduction mechanisms. In addition, we show that the demon's inability to create a higher temperature gradient due to information loss is a universal consequence that applies to all quantum systems undergoing a quantum jump, resulting in a fundamental challenge of using quantum information to drive a chemical or thermal gradient efficiently.

of benchmark tasks representing both simple and complex scenarios are made
publicly available to promote advanced reinforcement learning research and
development. Furthermore, to address the challenge of modeling human

where prolonged, uninterrupted feedback sessions compromise human productivity,

To address this challenge, we've developed DART, a framework for human-in-the-loop 
learning with flexible feedback duration, capable of adapting to both prolonged 
and intermittent feedback sessions. 
For DART to operate during both extended and brief feedback sessions, we've incorporated multiple trial learning sessions, allowing DART to excel in both scenarios. 
Experimentation with DART has demonstrated its capacity for human-in-the-loop 
learning across both prolonged and brief feedback sessions, outperforming 
human performance in both instances. 
The developed framework is versatile and can be applied to any dataset, 
also showcasing its effectiveness when combined with diverse evaluation metrics. 
Further, DART has been found to successfully learn from feedback sessions 
as short as 10 seconds, while also handling prolonged sessions lasting up to 
7 hours, demonstrating its capacity for human-in-the-loop learning 
across both prolonged and brief feedback sessions.

Linking small knowledge bases to large ones is crucial for updating the knowledge graphs' scope, but currently, most graph embedding models struggle with accurately matching entities from these smaller bases. This challenge arises because these models are primarily optimized for predicting relations between well-connected entities within large knowledge graphs, rather than identifying entities that are isolated or less well-connected. As a result, there are significant gaps in the tail of the distribution of predicted scores. To address this issue, we propose a novel method called Disentangled In-Between Similarity Learning, which uses intermediate probes to extract entity representations from smaller bases that are similar in nature to those derived from large knowledge graphs. By utilizing in-batch similarities, we refine these representations by minimizing the distance between similar entities within each batch, thereby disentangling the representations and eliminating the gaps in the predicted scores. As a result, we achieve substantial improvements in accuracy on the task of linking small knowledge bases to large ones, outperforming state-of-the-art baselines and establishing new benchmarks in the domain of entity-level similarity. As further contributions, we examined the challenge of linking small knowledge bases from a theoretical perspective, established a publicly accessible dataset that includes entity representations for over 1 million entities within the YAGO3 dataset, and provided practical guidelines on optimizing the loss functions used in our proposed method. As results, we found that the entailed gaps in the distribution of predicted scores are highly invariant across different knowledge graphs, and that the task of linking small knowledge bases can be benchmarked against a set of easily replicable entity-level similarity challenges. As achievements, we outperformed the state-of-the-art baselines by 8.9% on the entity-level similarity challenge and achieved 82.5% accuracy on the linking small knowledge bases task. As additional findings, we found that the disentangled representations are highly discriminative, and that the proposed method excels in predicting the subgraph connectivity of the target entities prior to linking. As results on the entity-level similarity challenge, we achieved 82.5% accuracy overall, and specifically achieved 82.1% accuracy in predicting entities that are connected to at least one entity within large knowledge graphs, 83.5% accuracy in predicting entities that are connected to at least five other entities within large knowledge graphs, and 61.7% accuracy in predicting entities that are connected to at least one entity within small knowledge bases. To confirm this assumption, we employed both ultrafast spectroscopy and molecular dynamics to investigate the perovskite exciton. Our findings reveal that the exciton becomes delocalized due to the percolation of halogen anions. This delocalization is followed by a localization process driven by the percolation of lead cations, which occurs on a similar timescale. being streamlined by a unified framework that calculates the energy and

tracks the performance of tasks such as data preprocessing, model training,
evaluation, and inference, as well as system administration, using metrics
derived from the Monodor utility scheduling framework. DL-Prod allows for the
computation of the energy and productivity of tasks using a set of predefined
metrics, which can be combined to produce well-known metrics such as
flops/second and watts. The framework supports multiple productivity metrics,
including model accuracy, dataset size, and the number of images processed
per second, and provides a product metric that represents the efficiency of
each task. Additionally, DL-Prod includes a feature that assigns higher
priority to tasks with higher product metrics, allowing for more efficient
resource allocation. The framework has been used to analyze the energy and
productivity of various DL experiments, and has provided insights that can
be used to optimize task scheduling and reduce energy consumption. The code
for DL-Prod is available for download. 

The DL-Prod framework has been applied to an extensive dataset comprising
2,412 neural network training experiments, covering various model architectures
and datasets, with corresponding productivity and energy consumption metrics.
However, a significant majority (around 79%) of the experiments lacked
completed productivity measurements. The analysis revealed that data from
high-productivity experiments (with productivity values greater than 104) was
inadequate, while there was an overabundance of data from low-productivity
experiments (with productivity values less than 104). It was also found that
researchers tend to prioritize training tasks with high productivity, but often
overlook measuring productivity for such tasks, and typically do not resume
partial experiments due to data consistency issues, resulting in significant
waste of computing resources and energy consumption. 

To mitigate these issues, DL-Prod proposes an energy-aware task scheduling
policy called Productivity-First Scheduling (PFS), which assigns higher
priority to experiments with higher product metrics, with the goal of
efficiently utilizing computing resources and reducing energy consumption. 

We observed that PFS can efficiently schedule experiments in the aforementioned
dataset, but the effectiveness of this policy requires further investigation. 

The proposed PFS policy has the potential to reduce computing resource utilization
and energy consumption during experiment scheduling, but may lead to experiment

healthcare providers, offering valuable insights through data analysis that
can inform treatment decisions. Despite the benefits, EHRs pose significant
security risks as they contain sensitive patient information, making it
essential to prioritize privacy protection while enabling data-sharing and
analysis. We investigate the feasibility of applying differential privacy, a
well-established framework for privacy preservation, to EHR analysis. Our
evaluation using real-world data from the MIMIC-III critical care database
demonstrates that standard DP techniques can result in inaccurate predictions,
offering a motivation to explore more effective privacy-preserving methods
such as federated learning and secure multi-party computation. We illustrate
the potential of these approaches by applying them to a representative
classification problem involving EHR data, finding that they can strike a
balance between preserving privacy and maintaining model performance. Our work
provides a starting point and a framework for evaluating privacy in healthcare
analytics, encouraging researchers and practitioners to explore and assess
privacy-preserving methods for EHR analysis.  Finally, we highlight several
challenges and potential research directions in this domain.  We also make our
code available to facilitate further innovation and replication of our work. 
We observe that in recent years, there has been growing interest in
machine learning for healthcare, but often little consideration is given to
an important aspect: data privacy. We aim to bridge this gap by delving into
the challenges of applying privacy-preserving machine learning in healthcare and
providing other researchers with a set of best practices to consider. We also
make the most of this opportunity to offer a review of healthcare machine
learning, exploring potential research directions and highlighting areas where
healthcare and machine learning can benefit from each other.  We illustrate
our point with a set of examples, highlighting models and datasets that
could be of interest to the research community and potentially for replication
and further innovation.  We also make our code available to facilitate this
process.  We believe that our work can contribute to the advancement of
healthcare machine learning and encourage other researchers to join us in this
endeavor.  We also open-source our code to facilitate further innovation and
replication of our work.

Research known as learner choice studies investigates how allowing students to decide between written and verbal tutorial instructions affects their learning. We conducted an experiment where half of the students could choose between text and video instructions for solving geometric puzzles, while the other half received video instructions as standard procedure. The results showed that students who chose video instructions successfully completed more puzzles. However, when considering both successful and unsuccessful attempts together, there was no significant difference in completion rate. Additionally, there wasn't a notable difference in the time it took to complete each puzzle. These findings suggest that allowing students to select between text and video instructions can lead to improved performance with minimal additional cost in terms of time and effort. Therefore, we recommend incorporating learner choice studies into experiments that involve interactive learning environments and involve students making decisions that impact their learning process. We also explored how student preferences and decision-making behaviors evolve over time, as well as the factors that influence their choices and performance. The results revealed that students generally prefer video instructions but can be swayed by difficulties encountered with either format. We found no evidence of a learning history effect, where past experiences influence current decisions and performance. We observed that students who choose video instructions and those who prefer text instructions exhibit distinct patterns in their completion rates, suggesting that they utilize different problem-solving strategies. We provide actionable insights and data for future researcher investigating learner choice in educational settings. We propose a framework to enhance the scope and generalizability of future learner choice studies, and we make available our experiment's methods, data, and analysis to promote the replication and extension of this research. We discovered that students overestimate their own ability to apply the geometric reasoning rules and developed a metric to quantify this phenomenon, known as rule fluency. We found that rule fluency is linked to completion rate and influenced by choice condition and preference. We explored incorporating an additional variable, student self-assessment, into the model explaining completion rates and found that it is a significant predictor, alongside choice condition and preference. We developed a theoretical framework to describe the relationship between these variables and propose future research to test it further. We demonstrated that student self-assessment is a valuable tool to enhance learning when incorporated into choice-based educational interactions. We discovered that students are capable of articulating the differences between video instructions that are effective and those that are not, and we found a strong correlation between their ability to do so and their future completion rates. The difficulty is compounded when the detection language includes a significant amount of paraphrased content from the source language. To tackle this issue, a high-degree of semantic similarity is necessary between the source and detection languages, making the detection of Chinese documents plagiarized from non-Chinese sources particularly complicated. This problem is further complicated by the fact that existing anti-plagiarism systems are designed to detect intra-language plagiarism, and typically rely on the vast amount of available training data in that specific language. In contrast, the amount of training data available for a non-Chinese source language is significantly limited. To address this challenge, we propose a new approach called Cross-Lingual Anti-Plagiarism (CLAP), which leverages the knowledge of multiple source languages to detect plagiarism in a new model trained on the detection language alone. In our implementation, we develop a new multi-source hard negative mining technique to create high-quality fake examples mimicking the format of non-Chinese source languages. These fake examples are used to train a new non-Chinese model that can identify plagiarism in documents from any non-Chinese source languages. Our CLAP approach achieves a 10% improvement in detection accuracy and an 8% improvement in precision over the existing state-of-the-art methods, and outperforms a baseline model trained on a single non-Chinese language by 5% in both metrics. Our study also reveals that incorporating additional source languages in the hard negative mining process leads to a further improvement of 3% in both metrics. Our CLAP approach has been successfully applied to a large-scale real-world Chinese dataset containing over 200K documents, and has been deployed in a real-world anti-plagiarism system by Tencent. In addition, we have successfully detected over 1.5 million pieces of Chinese documents plagiarized from non-Chinese sources, and reported our findings to the relevant parties. In total, we have reported 724 cases of plagiarism involving well-known authors, researchers and companies, including those from the top 100 universities in China, and 304 cases of plagiarism involving project descriptions of research projects funded by the National Science Foundation of China. The problem known as $p$-tuple list coloring of a graph $G$ involves determining if a specific assignment of colors to the vertices of $G$, where each vertex is provided with a list of allowed colors, can be replaced by a subset $C$ of the original coloring $C$, such that $C$ is equivalent to a subset of the original coloring containing $p$ elements, where the relationship between $C$ and $C$ holds for every one-to-one correspondence between the elements of the two sets. This research introduces a new concept called the recognition problem of $p$-tuple list colorability, which involves identifying if a given graph possesses the property of $p$-tuple list colorability, where the number $p$ is also determined during the recognition process. The graph $K_4^+$, obtained by adding a new edge to the complete graph $K_4$, is shown to have the ability to be $p$-tuple list colored for $p=3$ when $p$ is less than 4, but there exists a value of $p$ greater than or equal to 4 for which the graph $K_4^+$ cannot be $p$-tuple list colored. The recognition problem of $p$-tuple list colorability is also found to be decidable for $p=2$, while it becomes undecidable for $p$ equal to or greater than 3. Moreover, the complexity of the recognition problem of $p$-tuple list colorability is shown to be NP-complete for $p=2$. The notion of the recognition problem of $p$-tuple list colorability is found to be closely related to another concept called the homomorphism problem of list homomorphism, which involves determining if a specific mapping between two graphs, where each vertex of the first graph is provided with a list of allowed colors, can be replaced by a subset of the original mapping, which contains a homomorphism of the second graph. The Higgs-strahlung process, a crucial channel for studying the Higgs boson, will be investigated at CLIC using the Higgs-jet tagging tool to eliminate major background sources. A key challenge in developing this technique is the complex nature of multi-body final states, which necessitates a sophisticated approach to distinguish signal events from background events. In this paper, we introduce a deep learning algorithm known as DeepFullyConnectedNetwork (DFCN), which demonstrates exceptional performance in identifying signal events in the presence of background events when applying tight selection criteria. Combining optical and infrared observations of near-Earth asteroid 2011 AG5 allowed the characterization of its phase curve, which in turn facilitated the determination of its size and shape. Additionally, by observing the asteroid at varying distances from the Earth, scientists were able to gather information about its composition and light reflecting properties. The data collected suggests that 2011 AG5 has a dynamic shape caused by its slow rotation period and gravitational forces from nearby objects, potentially including a large triaxial moon. The composition of the asteroid reveals a dark surface with properties similar to some carbonaceous asteroids, specifically a water absorption feature that may indicate the presence of hydrated minerals, which could also be affected by the nearby objects. Furthermore, the discovery of this asteroid system offers several potential targets for the Earth, Moon, and Mars interception in the coming decades, with 2011 AG5 being particularly relevant for a deep space gravity probe in 2029. Recently, researchers have been studying  non-biological systems, such as spin glasses, superconductors, and  anti-ferromagnets, that exhibit critical behavior due to their complex  network structures. The consequences of this folding process lead to  prion protein aggregation, a phenomenon responsible for prion disease.  On the other hand, the folding of the prion protein might be prevented  if the energy landscape of the protein can be altered in a way that  disrupts the folding process, thus providing a potential approach  for developing therapeutic prion disease treatments. multi-dimensional negative log-likelihood functions, specifically those arising from data with non-normal distributions, in order to calculate quantiles. Traditional methods for approximating quantiles rely on the central limit theorem and do not account for the skewing effect of non-normal data on the quantile estimator. As a result, they can lead to significant inaccuracies in the estimation of tail probabilities and quantiles for data sets that are substantially non-normal. We explore alternative approximations that are robust to non-normality and often more precise, leveraging the saddlepoint method that utilizes the characteristic function instead of the distribution function. However, the saddlepoint method typically requires one-dimensional calculations, but for complex datasets, we must employ multi-dimensional processing, resulting in less intuitive output. To address this, we develop new graphics tools to illustrate the accuracy of these approximations and the behavior of the quantile estimator. We also investigate multiple criteria to select the number of dimensions to approximate, given the computational resources available, and provide a metric that forecasts approximate computation time based on a set of sample data. Finally, we apply our methods to analyze the accuracy of quantile estimators in various datasets, including those from fields such as economics, engineering, medicine, and social sciences.

, Fast R-CNN, Faster R-CNN, and FRCNN++ have dominated object detection challenges due to their high accuracy.  These methods rely on a network called a region proposal network (RPN) to generate proposals for the Fast R-CNN network to classify and refine them.  RPNs are single-task networks that focus solely on generating proposals.  Fast R-CNN and FRCNN++ use two separate networks for proposal generation and object classification and refinement.  Since both networks are necessary for overall system evaluation,  there has been little incentive to improve RPNs independently.  In response to the lack of RPN optimization,  our research introduces a Unified RPN (U-RPN) that allows for end-to-end object detection training.  Datasets are oversampled to focus on challenging proposals,  enhancing proposal quality.  Our U-RNN approach outperforms two-lane network counterparts in multiple benchmark challenges. This requirement implies that the model must capture the underlying causal relationships between events and be able to reason about these relationships to predict the effects of specific actions. To evaluate the causal reasoning abilities of language models, we developed a new test that assesses their ability to understand cause-and-effect relationships and use this understanding to predict the consequences of those causes. Our results show that single-shot models outperform few-shot and fine-tuned models in our causal reasoning test, but surprisingly, neither model performs significantly better than chance based on our current data. This finding suggests that there may be room for further research into language models' ability to understand causal relationships and use this understanding to predict the consequences of those causes. One potential limitation of our test is that it relies heavily on static textual information, but physical action-effect relationships are often more effectively conveyed through a combination of visual and semantic information. Therefore, we believe that models tested in this way may not perform as well as they would in more comprehensive, more realistic scenarios. This study focuses on the Paschen beta indices, a measure of stellar emission in a specific spectral range related to magnetic activity, to understand the behavior of low-mass stars in different stages of evolution.  By analyzing a vast dataset covering a wide spectral range for stars in the mass range of 0.1 to 0.6 solar masses, researchers discovered that the Paschen beta absorption depth is most closely correlated with H-alpha full width at half maximum, showing that it serves as a reliable indicator for measuring the starspin period relationship. In addition, a comparison with the Sun-like G-type main-sequence star Proximus, which is expected to become a red dwarf in the distant future, showed that its expected increase in activity is likely minimal, possibly indicating a decrease in activity itself as a star evolves from main-sequence to the red giant branch.  In order to accurately model the behavior of absorption in this specific spectral range, a new equation for the starspin period relationship was derived and found to be in alignment with other activity indicators, suggesting that the physical mechanism governing the behavior of absorption in this range is closely linked to the conventional spectral range.  In the context of the upcoming James Webb Space Telescope observations of the nearest red giants and subgiants, it will be possible to study the behavior of low-mass stars with the aid of magnetic activity indicators like Paschen beta, even when such stars are no longer visible in the ultraviolet spectrum.  In the search for exoplanets, researchers can utilize the relationship between the stars spin and the behavior of absorption in this specific spectral range to prioritize targets with the most significant activity levels, increasing the chances of detecting planetary systems.  In order to accomplish this, a new database featuring the Paschen beta indices of low-mass stars was created and is available for public access, along with a new algorithm capable of deriving other activity indicators from the spectra of the stars studied. These studies are conducted by a team of researchers who acquired nearly complete abundance measurements for hundreds of galaxies observed with HUDACS and nearly a thousand galaxies observed with 4-ORC. The oxygen abundance was derived from analyzing light emitted by the galaxies, specifically from analyzing the spectra of light that  HUDACS and 4-ORC detected in their observations. We derive a nonlinear equation describing the development of zonal modes and demonstrating the transfer of energy from these modes to a state of equilibrium. We demonstrate that this process occurs through the excitation of secondary zonal modes and the emission of internal waves, and validate our findings through direct numerical simulations. We show that our model accurately predicts the development of zonal flows not only in deep systems but also in those with limited depth, and that it correctly accounts for the formation of step-like structures. We also demonstrate that our model is robust in scenarios where rotation has varying intensity. We find that the transfer of energy to zonal flows occurs most efficiently when rotation has a moderate rather than very weak or very strong influence. We study the parameters of our model to understand the mechanisms responsible for the formation of zonal flows, and we find that our model provides an efficient pathway for energy transfer when there is an overlap between zonal flow and internal wave modes, and when zonal flow modes are excited through the decay of other wave modes. We find that the most efficiently transferred energy is carried by the lowest wavenumber zonal modes, and that the secondary zonal modes responsible for the transfer are determined by the system's parameters, and that they can be both down- and wavenumber-shifted in relation to the primary zonal mode. We validate our findings through direct numerical simulations, and we demonstrate that our model accurately accounts for the development of zonal flows in all scenarios considered. We show that our model can be simplified into a universal form applicable to all systems, and that it is governed by a single dimensionless parameter, and that this parameter fully accounts for the diversity of the systems we study. We demonstrate that this parameter controls both the efficiency and rate of energy transfer to zonal flows, and that it drives the formation of step-like structures, and that it accounts for the distinct features of the systems we study. We show that this parameter has both an inner and an outer component, and that the inner component fully captures the behavior of the system at its core, and that the outer component captures the behavior of the system's extended parts, and that together they capture the system's overall dynamics, and that they operate in unison to drive the energy transfer to zonal flows, and that they operate in harmony to drive the formation of step-like structures, and that they operate in concert to drive the energy transfer to zonal flows,

To monitor the infestation levels and treatment effects, sampling of mites from individual bees is common practice. However, the accuracy of these measurements can be impacted by both the sampling method used and the analysis technique employed. In this study, we examined the bee population model developed by Crain (1981) to evaluate the efficacy of the fixed-sample-size (FSS) method, specifically looking at the impact of sampling on estimates of infestation levels and the associated confidence intervals. Our analysis considered both the number of mites present on each bee and the sampling method's influence on the derived estimates. We created the modified FSS method, which takes into account the overestimation caused by sampling without replacement, and found it to be more precise than the standard FSS method. To determine the required sample size for the modified FSS method, we used the Wald confidence interval estimator and found it to be more conservative than the estimates provided by Crain (1981). Nonetheless, our results indicate that the modified FSS method yields more reliable estimates than the conventional FSS method, and the suggested sample size is sufficient to maintain the desired level of precision and confidence. ological and geometric analysis of the base space of a torus corresponding to a completely hyperbolic group. Initially, we present a concise overview of the torus itself, including its geometry and fundamental group. Subsequently, we examine the base space, commencing with its geometric representation when the torus group has more than one conjugacy class of maximal parabolic subgroups. These subgroups correspond to the boundaries of its group's Cayley graph, thereby defining the base space as a quotient of the torus' geometric representation. If there is only one such conjugacy class, the base space is equivalent to the torus itself. We then discuss how a base space associated with a torus group resembles a twisted version of that torus, describing it through a set of twisted directions. These directions are defined by the orientations of its group's boundary components, which determine the base space's unique geometry. Furthermore, we establish that a base space can be thought of as a torus that has been 'twisted' or 'bent', resulting in unique geometric properties. We also explore specific examples of base spaces derived from well-known groups, including Kleinian groups, hyperbolic surface group and some arithmetic groups. Subsequently, we investigate the underlying principles of these base spaces, identifying the requirements for them to be compact, orientable or of a specific genus. We also introduce the novel term 'bent' to describe base spaces, emphasizing that this term is not officially part of geometric group theory terminology. However, we propose that it 'bends' conventional thinking and could be shortened to 'base' in everyday conversation. has significantly altered how individuals access and disseminate information, ultimately affecting the diffusion process. We have investigated the online information diffusion process using various technological means and found it to be influenced by the type of technology employed, with notable differences evident. For example, the diffusion process was slower on Twitter than Facebook, likely due to differences in user behavior and platform features. Furthermore, the diffusion process varied across different types of technology, with factors such as the level of anonymity and the amount of relevant information readily available playing a crucial role. We discovered that information diffused more slowly when users required a level of effort to access it and that the degree of overposting, or posting irrelevant content, had a distinct impact on the diffusion process. We investigated multiple combinations of these factors to develop actionable guidelines for creators and communicators, highlighting the importance of considering the technology used to present information and the potential for overposting. By understanding the effects of different technologies on information diffusion, communicators can tailor their message's presentation to achieve greater impact. We have made our dataset and methods publicly available to facilitate further research into online information diffusion processes. As a consequence of this evolution, the power system infrastructure has become increasingly vulnerable to cyber threats. Consequently, detecting anomalous traffic within the power system network has become a pressing concern for both network operators and security analysts, who require efficient identification methods to detect malicious activity and generate alerts for further investigation. To address this challenge, we present a method for real-time traffic anomaly detection within power system networks. Initially, we collect normal traffic data and train a one-class support vector machine model to define the normal network protocol buffer (NPB) format. Next, we use this model to detect anomalies in real-time traffic data. Our proposed method is implemented in an actual power system network and compared with alternative techniques to demonstrate its effectiveness. Results show that our method achieves a high accuracy and outperforms alternative techniques in terms of detection performance and computational efficiency. Our model's small size enables it to run on low-cost hardware, making it suitable for deployment in smart grids and other large-scale power system networks. Furthermore, our method detects anomalies at the application layer, resulting in more precise identification of malicious activity. To facilitate reproducibility, we provide a model repository containing data, implementation details, and results to guide researchers and practitioners in executing and evaluating this method. Additionally, we develop a traffic anomaly detection platform, which includes our proposed method and an NPB format, to provide a reference for practitioners seeking to deploy this technology in their own networks. This platform is available online and can be used to detect anomalies in power system networks and other network types. In conjunction with this work, we publish a new dataset called the Power System Network Anomaly Dataset (PSNA-DS), containing 18 million traffic packets collected from a power system network, to serve as a resource for researchers developing new traffic anomaly detection methods. This dataset is available on the dataset platform mentioned above. In addition to presenting our proposed method, we provide a detailed review of recent research related to traffic anomaly detection, identifying key challenges and potential solutions. To facilitate further research, we outline a set of requirements for detection algorithms and suggest multiple approaches, including supervised and unsupervised methods, protocol-based and feature-based techniques, layer-based and packet-based strategies, and traditional and machine learning techniques. We discuss the advantages and disadvantages of each approach and highlight the need for additional research in this field. Consequently, we propose future research directions, including developing new methods to detect anomalies in networks with varying traffic patterns and identifying the most effective features for detecting anomalies
